# 4. Steel and Fire

*Pages PDF 87-120*

**I** IVI 

## **Steel and Fire**
## Dwarf Engineering
_‘The steam-powered tanks produced by Leonardo da Miragliano make for the high water mark of our military engineering genius. Built in 2512 IC, over 500 years ago. Since then we have not advanced our knowledge and techniques — we can hardly maintain Leonardo’s tanks and barely glean his design. Meanwhile, Dwarfs produce innovations with such ease that I feel ashamed to call myself an engineer. What is von Brunel’s sub-hydro velocipator but a flimsy wooden plagiarism of their vastly superior nautilus? Bazalgette’s celebrated cloaca of Kislev a pale imitation of plumbing thought unremarkable in any backwater Dwarf mine. Todmeister’s harquebus an unwieldy and slow single-function device compared to the repeating handgun of Mad Makaisson? There are days when I think of packing it in and working in a tannery.’_ 

– Stefan Wenckler, co-creator of the pigeon bomb, in one of his self-reflective moods. 

The Dwarfs are famed for their mastery of technology. From massive feats of civil engineering to intricate devices that can fit in the palm of a hand, the technology of Dwarfs is celebrated for its fine workmanship, durability, and reliability of function. Great works of the Dwarfs include the massive pumping mechanism incorporated into the Vloedmuur around Marienburg,the experimental warpfire distillery pioneered by Burlok Damminson, and the massive airship Spirit of Grungni built by Malakai Makaisson. There are four key traits that set dwarf technology apart from that of others. 

## **A Projection of Power**
At the end of the Golden Age, when Dwarf made war on Elf, the Dwarfs were far more numerous and could field armies equal in numbers to those of Ulthuan. Steel axes and Dwarf determination were enough to drive the Elves from the Old World. 

But the Fall that followed was a disaster from which the Dwarfs have never really recovered. Numberless Dwarfs died when hold after hold fell to the hordes of Orcs, Goblins, and Skaven. Beset from all sides above and below the earth, more Dwarfs died at the holds that remained than could ever be replaced. Though the situation started to stabilise after years of hard fighting through the Dwarfs’ sheer grit and refusal to die, Karaz Ankor could see the runes upon the wall. If something didn’t change, the Dwarf empire would fall. 

Whether through luck, an ingenuity born of desperation, or inspiration from Grungni, many things changed. First came the development of black powder. Used first in the mines to fracture large ore seams, the Dwarfs soon realised it could also kill enemies by the cartload. Then came the discovery of ways to cast metal so that it could be used with black powder to create cannons and handguns, letting Karaz Ankor’s armies take its power to the battlefield, a small crew of gunners having the force of a regiment. The use of gunpowder weaponry in the hands of the Dwarfs dates back to -370 IC, when cannons were employed against the Orcs in the Battle of Blackwater. 

Steam engines further amplified Dwarf power. The invention of the steam-powered gyrocopter gave the Dwarfs mobility they had never enjoyed in the past, and its steam gun wreaked havoc upon the greenskins. The steam-driven tunnel borer allowed the Dwarfs to dig deeper and further than they ever had, both in search of precious metals and minerals, and to attack the Skaven in their tunnels where and when they least expected it. Behind many of these devices, precision clockwork mechanisms ensured a reliability far surpassing the mechanisms of manling craft. 

While unable to bring about final victory, each new innovation helped level the field for the Dwarfs against their enemies, meaning Karaz Ankor not only survived another day, but could even push back. 

**I** IVI 

## **Tradition**
For all the wondrous devices, the Dwarf Craft Guilds, and Dwarf society beyond them, are very conservative. Conservative in ways that a Talabheim matriarch would consider stodgy. The Elders regard innovation with suspicion, and new ideas are accepted only grudgingly, even after years — even centuries! — of design, testing, re-design, and re-testing. Even when an invention shows exceptional promise, as gunpowder did, many masters and clan elders refuse to accept that deployment of the device will improve their situation _’._ 

This almost reactionary wariness of anything new is a product both of Dwarf culture and the dangers facing it. 

Dawi revere the Ancestor Gods, particularly Grungni, Valaya, Grimnir, and, among the Engineer clans, Morgrim, the ‘First Engineer’. Before returning to the depths of the earth, these Ancestors taught the Dwarfs all that they would need to know to survive and prosper. To claim that one has invented a device that does the job better than what an Ancestor God created sounds like an insult born of hubris. 

On top of cultural and religious pressure, the desire to stick with the tried-and-true comes from a fear of making fatal mistakes. Karaz Ankor is under constant pressure on all sides from greenskins, Chaos Dwarfs, and Skaven. If they’re not actively besieging, they’re plotting and watching and waiting for another opening to attack. The Dawi can ill-afford to lose more holds — or more Dwarfs! — so the risks inherent in trying something new combine with natural Dwarf traditionalism to make most inventions too chancey to try. 

## **‘Magnificent Sven’ Hasselfriesian**
Dwarf culture does have its renegades, including in the Engineer clans. Notorious among these is Sven Hasselfriesian, Master Engineer, who has the distinction of having his name in the Book of Grudges of two holds, Karaz-a-Karak and Barak Varr. Initially trained at Zhufbar and then enrolled in the Craft Guild of Karaz-a-Karak, Sven developed a reputation for crazy, half-baked experiments that wrecked more than one workshop. Threatened with permanent sanction if he didn’t mend his ways, he convinced a friend, Burlok Damminsson, to work with him in an old, forgotten workshop. This ended in disaster when Sven’s latest invention, a steam-powered miner, exploded. The blast nearly killed Sven and cost Burlok an arm. Though they escaped the severest punishment, the Council of Elders ordered the humiliating public destruction of all their inventions. 

Not discouraged, Sven decided to go someplace where his talents would be appreciated, and so moved to Barak Varr, which had a more open-minded reputation. Here he designed a radical new engine that ran on alcohol vapours and mounted it in a ship he christened the _‘Voltsvagn’_ . Instead of being embraced, his new design was seen as a threat by the jealous engineers of the shipbuilding clans, who used their influence to convince the Dwarf king to expel Sven and suppress his invention. Before the invention could be smashed, Sven absconded with his own ship and sailed off into the Black Gulf. 

After a long voyage round the Old World, Sven reached Marienburg, where he gained an audience with Arkat Fooger, head of one of the city’s ten Houses that sit on its ruling Directorate. Flatlander Dwarfs are dangerously open to innovation, as any Dawi of Karaz Ankor would say, and the wily old banker was intrigued by the potential of Sven’s invention. With generous funding from House Fooger, Sven put together a crew of Dwarfs and Humans and set off for no less a target than Lustria, promising to bring back to Fooger a boatload of gold. 

Since then no word was heard of the _Voltsvagn_ , and Arkat Fooger came to assume his investment was lost. Just as he was about to write it off his books, Sven and his ship (and most of his crew) chugged into Marienburg harbour, the ship battered and barely afloat with all the gold it carried. No longer known as ‘Crazy Sven’, he earned a new name that day, ‘Magnificent Sven’. 

**I** IVI 

## **Secretive**

- _‘That’s on a “need to know” basis, manling. And you’ve got no need to know.’_ 

   - Zhufbar Engineer to a curious visitor 

Dwarfs are by nature a secretive folk. Though for those who have experienced the tight-lipped ways of Dawi in the Empire, the secretiveness of the Dwarfs of Karaz Ankor is still impressive, and among the Engineers most of all. Ask one the time of day, and he’ll probably give you a glare and grumble suspiciously. Gruff humour may account for some of this attitude, but a genuine desire that others mind their own business is common to such Dwarfs. 

A more forthcoming Dwarf, however, may tell you that it is the natural reaction to thousands of years of others trying to steal what you have. Treasure, runelore, technological discoveries — everything that represents both the patrimony of the Ancestor Gods and what the Dwarfs have worked countless generations for. With seemingly everyone else trying to take all that the Dawi value, including their lives, it is no wonder that Dwarfs are reticent to talk about what they have. 

For the kings of the karaks and the elders of the Engineer clans, secretiveness is also a vital matter of ‘hold security’. Given their reliance on technological superiority to make up for their lesser numbers, they cannot afford to let their methods fall into the claws of cunning foes, such as the Skaven. The workshops zealously guard their knowledge from espionage, even preparing explosives to destroy them, should the hold be invaded. 

## **A Covert Operation**
A Dwarf gyrocopter secret mission crashed in the eastern World’s Edge mountains near the Dark Lands, and the High King fears what might happen if it and its cargo fall into the hands of the Skaven or the Chaos Dwarfs. The Characters are an elite band of Dwarf Rangers, either all-Dawi or mixed Dawi and Dawikoni, sent deep into enemy territory to recover the cargo and make sure the gyrocopter is destroyed. 

In addition to the expected dangers of the journey — greenskins and trolls — a band of Skaven Stormvermin are escorting a Clan Skyre Warlock-Engineer to the same site. Who arrives first? Can the Characters accomplish their mission and escape? And what secrets was the now-deceased pilot carrying? 

## **Workshop Culture**
Dwarfs take pride in the craftsmanship, regarding each item they make as not just a tool, but as a work of art, an expression of the ‘Dawi way’. Instead of mass production of basic items on an assembly line, Dwarf Master Engineers supervise the construction of each piece from start to finish in crafts halls, where journeymen and apprentices labour under his or her watchful eye. Time is almost never a factor, as quality is far more important. While there are standards maintained by the Engineers Guild, Dwarf artisans still have wide leeway and strive to make their items as individual as possible in both decoration and function. This often shows in the small details, invisible to an outsider’s eye, unless an aficionado, but evident to a Dawi engineer. A clan elder can often tell at a glance what hold and from which master’s tools an item came. 

This attention to craftsmanship and small-scale manufacturing comes at a cost, however. When combined with Dawi conservatism and secretiveness, the workshop culture contributes to the slow pace of production and innovation. Dwarf craftworkers of Karaz Ankor are loath, to say the least, to share secrets even with each other, a reticence that works against Karaz Ankor’s long-term interests. Some have even been known to take their journals with them to the tomb, destroying all copies but the one. The Dwarf who takes over the workshop, whether another master or a promoted journeyman, must start all over. 

**I** IVI 

## Gromril
## Outside Karaz Ankor
Like the rulers of Karaz Ankor, the Engineers Guild and their associated clans in the Dwarf empire have strained relations with the Engineer clans in the western holds and, moreso, with the ‘flatlander’ guilds in the towns and cities of the Empire. Though often a distinction without a difference to Humans, Elves, and Halflings, the Karaz Ankor guild chides the others for being too open to innovation, complaining that they have ‘no respect for tradition. Worse, they are far too willing to share knowledge with Imperial guilds. Manlings are far too prone to corruption, they say, and there is too great a risk of the Dawi’s secrets being turned against them. 

The western holds and the Imperial Dwarf clans, on the other hand, think Karaz-a-Karak is foolishly shortsighted. Not that they intend to give the manlings everything, but sharing with them when it seems advisable is only good sense. After all, they sometimes remind their cousins, it was only because of the manlings that Karaz Ankor could repel Chaos in the Incursion. And, as the Dwarfs of the Empire’s cities are quick to point out, they have lived among the manlings for thousands of years. It would be not only foolish, but an insult to Kurgan’s oath not to share knowledge and techniques with them. 

Most of the time, there are little more than arguments in Khazalid that eventually peter out. Sometimes, however, they result in a genuine rift and the laying of grudges, particularly when the Empire is in turmoil and the Dwarfs’ position there seems endangered. 

_’Keep your coin, manling. This gromril axe is worth more than all the gold in the counting houses of your stinking city.’_ 

## — a Karaz Ankor Dwarf to a Marienburg Collector
The hardest metal known, gromril is the greatest treasure of the Dawi, and they would sooner part with everything else than give up an ounce of it to a non-Dwarf. To say it is valuable to them would be an injustice, for that implies a Dwarf could — or would — set a price on it. No Dwarf can. To the Dawi, gromril is their birthright, the Ancestors’ greatest gift to them. Their reverence for gromril is shown by the other name they give it, _‘Grungni’s Blood’_ . 

Dwarf Law reserves the wearing and wielding of gromril to just a few — the Dwarf kings of the holds and the heads of the noble clans, their guards, and the elite warriors of a hold’s army. Gromril also serves to decorate the stones that seal the tombs of the Dwarf kings, its eternal lustre reflecting the eternal glory of the tomb’s occupant. 

Dwarfs spare no effort to recover gromril that falls into others’ possession. If by accident or with no malicious intent, the Dwarfs offer gold in exchange, making it clear that refusal would be unwise. Pity the poor fool greedy enough to steal gromril, however, for such a thief earns an eternal, deadly grudge, and the Dawi spare no effort to recover it. Even Dwarfs from other holds and Imperial towns hunt the thief, such is the hold gromril has over the Dawi heart. 

**I** IVI 

## **Gromril Mining**
In 657 IC a Dwarf prospector called Thori Gundrikson made a discovery in the lands around the Black Water. Veins of an unfamiliar metal were found in caves around the lake, as bright and incorruptible as silver, as workable as iron, and harder than any other metal known to engineers and alchemists alike. Karak Varn, already a major mining settlement famed for its gold production, became a hub of activity, as the new metal was pulled from the ground and transported to Zhufbar for smelting and working. 

Since then, the Dwarfs have ventured ever deeper in search of gromril, and the discovery of a new vein is met with joy in all the holds. But the extraction of gromril has become harder over the years. The Dwarfs of Karak Varn carved their tunnels and pits into the land around Black Water with heedless haste, and soon the mines were beset by disasters, flooding, cave ins, and incursions from Skaven and Night Goblins. It became increasingly difficult to work there and the hold was overrun by the enemies of the Dwarfs. 

Over the millennia, the Dwarfs have learned to mine, smelt, and work gromril into weapons and armour, secrets they have never revealed to anyone else. As the supply from Karak Varn has become increasingly difficult to find, and dangerous to extract and transport, the Dwarfs search far afield for more sources of the metal though, to their growing despair, the lands around Karak Varn seem to be the only natural source of the metal in the world. 

## **Gromril Armour**
Gromril armour is almost always only made for Dwarfs, as giving away Grungni’s gift is unthinkable to most. Only once or twice in all Dawi history has a suit been made for an outsider, that person having proven themself a true Dwarf friend. Gromril is rare, expensive, and difficult to work, but due to its unsurpassed hardness it is most commonly used in the construction of suits of armour, though such monumentally expensive suits are reserved for the mightiest Dwarf heroes and their elite tunnel fighters, the Ironbreakers. 

Gromril is a legendarily durable material, the most precious metal worked by Dwarfs. Items forged from gromril will not break, corrode, or lose their edge in almost all circumstances. In addition to other qualities possessed by a piece of armour a piece of gromril armour always possesses Fine 1 and Durable 4. 

Any attacks against locations protected by _Gromril_ armour do not inflict Critical Wounds if they roll a Critical. An attack can still inflict Critical Wounds if it inflicts the target Character to 0 Wounds, as normal. 

## **Gromril Weapons**
Gromril weapons are the finest known, and only the most skilled Dwarf smiths forge weapons from it. Meant for the Dwarfkings and their elite guards, gromril weapons are also given as gifts to the great heroes of Karaz Ankor after a legendary deed. Runesmiths will often inscribe runes of power on gromril weapons, making them even more fearsome. 

All gromril weapons, regardless of the presence of wounds, have the Durable 4 Quality. Axes will also have Damaging, while hammers have the Impact Quality. 

To work out the price of an item made from gromril double the base cost of the item seven times. So a sword (1 GC) would cost 128 GC if made from gromril. Really, this is a minimum price for an item that somehow made its way to market. Gromril items are regarded by Dwarfs as prized military and cultural assets and they do not part with such things lightly. 

## **The King’s Gift**
While exploring the wild foothills of the World’s Edge Mountains between Grenzstadt and the Blue Reach, Characters from the Empire strike it rich. Clearing a cave of Orcs, they find a gromril helmet made for an adult Human. A rare treasure, it was crafted long-ago for an Elector Count of Averland who had saved the heir of the Dwarf king of Karak Angazhar. The helm was lost when the Dwarf ambassador delivering it and his party were ambushed and slaughtered. Word of its discovery of course leaks out and the Characters find themselves beset by factions demanding its surrender. The current ElectorCount claims it as an heirloom of office. The Dwarfs of Karak Angazhar want it back, insisting it was only a loan to that particular Count. Agents of the Gold College see a rare opportunity to closely study gromril’s properties and claim it in the name of Imperial interests. Even the High King of Karaz Ankor demands it be handed over to him as a sacred treasure of the Dwarfs. 

Meanwhile, the helm itself is worth a fortune to the right buyer. Whom do the Characters please, and whom do they anger?

## New Weapon Qualities and Flaws
In addition to the Qualities and Flaws listed in **WFRP** , Dwarf Trappings may also have the _Crewed_ Flaw, _Salvo_ , or _Spread_ Qualities. 

## **Crewed (Rating)**
For this weapon to operate optimally, it must be crewed by the number of characters equal to its Rating, all with the relevant Ranged skill (e.g. a _Crewed (3)_ weapon requires 3 trained crew to operate efficiently). Only one crewmember can fire the weapon each Round, but additional crew can move or reload the weapon in their Turn. Misfires ( **WFRP Core Rulebook** ) damage all characters crewing the weapon, to a random hit location instead of the Primary Arm. 

A _Crewed_ weapon with insufficient crew doubles its _Reload_ Rating. In addition, the weapon gains the _Imprecise_ Flaw if it is short 2 or more crew, and the _Dangerous_ Flaw if it is short 3 or more crew. If this effect would duplicate Flaws the weapon already has, it inflicts −10 on Ranged Tests per duplicated Flaw. 

## **Salvo (Rating)**
A _Salvo_ weapon can be fired a number of times equal to its Rating before it needs to be reloaded. When shooting a _Salvo_ weapon, you can choose to fire a single shot (reducing Salvo by 1), or a batch of missiles (reducing _Salvo_ by the number of shots fired). Each missile fired after the first suffers a cumulative −10 on its Ranged Test (−10 for the second shot, −20 for the third shot, etc.). 

The _Reload_ Rating of a _Salvo_ weapon indicates the SLs required to increase its _Salvo_ by 1. A weapon’s _Salvo_ Rating cannot exceed the number listed in its profile. 

If a Dwarf _Salvo_ weapon Misfires ( **WFRP Core Rulebook** ) on a roll of 00, the crew suffers a number of hits equal to the weapon’s remaining _Salvo_ Rating (minimum 1). 

## **Spread (Rating)**
Weapons with the Spread Quality fire an expanding cloud of projectiles which may strike several targets. Depending on the range to the target, weapons with this Quality behave somewhat differently. 

- **Point Blank** : The shot targets a single individual. Add (Rating) to the weapon’s Damage. 

- **Short Range to Long Range** : The shot targets a single individual, and also the next (Rating) closest visible creatures. No two targets may be more than (Rating) yards apart. 

- **Extreme Range** : As for Short to Long Range but reduce the weapon’s Damage by (Rating).

## **Dwarf Ranged Weapons**
_’I call these “dual-purpose weapons”, lad. First, they kill a lot more of the enemy a lot faster. Second, they scare the tar out of the survivors.’_ 

## — a Karak Master Gunner Training a New Recruit
The Dawi are famous for their use of arquebuses and cannons, but few know the variety of their creations. Many of these are useful on the land, under the land, and on the sea. Dwarf ranged weaponry is constantly evolving, with “Drakefire” weapons the most recent development. Though regular handguns are dismissed by some elders as new-fangled nonsense, Dwarf blackpowder weapons are the most reliable ever invented, about as safe to use as any other weapon. 

## **Dwarf Ammunition**
For ease of use, the effects that ammunition have on the Range, Damage, Qualities, and Flaws of ranged weapons have been included in the weapon profiles listed in this chapter. When replacing spent ammunition for personal weapons, Dwarfs can buy 12 bullets and powder for 3/3, and 12 crossbow bolts for 5/- (both have Common Availability). 12 shots of Drakefire can either be purchased for 1GC (Rare Availability), or concocted as an Endeavour. 

Replacing ammunition for artillery is usually outside the budget of most adventuring parties. Characters determined to pay their way — or use variant ammunition like grapeshot, incendiary rounds, or animal carcasses — can find additional detail in **Up in Arms** (page 124).

## Ancestral Heirlooms
The following Trappings are rare treasures of the Dwarfs — few in number, and seldom used in battle, except by the most respected warriors. No Dwarf clan would ever willingly sell these heirlooms, though prices have been included for each, as a demonstration of their value in strictly material terms. 

## **Ancestral Heirlooms**
Item Price Enc Availability
Shield Platform 15 GC 4 n/a
Oathstone 25 GC 3 n/a

## **Shield Platform**
**Battle Standard** : Each Dwarf clan has a banner their warriors rally behind on the battlefield. Most are topped with metal heads, hanging medallions, or other ancestor badges, so those who fight beneath them never forget their predecessors are watching and judging them. Other customisations reflect the trade of the clan — banners of mining clans mount lanterns and candles, for example. Battle standards marked with protection runes extend the range of that protection rune to 12 yards. 

**Metal Foil Sheets** : These thin, flexible plates are used by Runescribes to inscribe a semi-permanent record — not as long-lasting as stone, but far more durable than paper. 

**Reckoner’s Log** : The grudges a Reckoner bears on their clients’ behalf are traditionally inscribed on stone tablets, and broken once satisfied. For practical reasons, many Reckoners record their grudges on books of parchment paper instead, which reduce their Encumbrance to 1. 

**Stone Tablets** : Despite their unwieldiness, stone tablets remain a popular choice for inscribing records that withstand the passage of time. 

**Trade Tools (Brewer)** : Pots, Buckets, Kettles, Mash Tun, Bottles, Barrels. Workshops (Breweries) include Mills, Tanks, Kegs, and Bottling Lines. 

**Trade Tools (Mason)** : Masonry Hammer, Chisels, Pick, Spikes, Steel Tongs. 

The Lords of several mountain holds prefer to be borne into battle by a pair of loyal retainers, upon a circular fighting platform fashioned like a stylised shield. This permits a rare height advantage over enemy infantry, and the opportunity to meet mounted warriors eye-to-eye. 

A Shield Platform requires three Characters to be effective — two bearers, of similar height, to carry the platform, and one rider to stand upon it. When determining if they are Overburdened ( **WFRP Core Rulebook** ), the bearers must split the Encumbrance of the rider (typically 10 Enc), their Trappings, and the Shield Platform itself (Enc 4) between them, in addition to the Encumbrance of their own Trappings. Consequently, Shield Platforms are usually borne by the strongest of a Dwarf Lord’s warriors, and even they rarely have the luxury of an arm free to defend themselves. 

Whilst atop the Shield Platform, the two bearers count as the rider’s mount per the rules for Mounted Combat ( **WFRP Core Rulebook** ), with the mount counting as Large Size. Unlike normal steeds, the rider cannot use the Ride Skill to make their shieldbearers run faster or jump! But Ride Skill Tests may be appropriate when determining if the rider keeps their balance aboard the platform (for example, if a bearer becomes _Entangled_ ). 

A Shield Platform can be inscribed with Armour, Talismanic, and Protection Runes. When fighting as a unit, both bearers and rider count as carrying those runes, with all corresponding benefits. The inspirational sight of a great warrior borne upon a Shield Platform may provide the rider a bonus to Perception, Leadership, or other Skill Tests, at the GM’s discretion. 

**I** IVI 

## **Oathstone**
Oathstone are a piece of a Dwarf ’s mountain home carried into battle with them, a carved rock inscribed with runes proclaiming the valour of the bearer, their ancestors, and their clan. They have been used since the War of Vengeance, when King Ironhandson of Karak Varn inscribed his personal rune on a boulder to denote his intent to defy his Elven pursuers during the Battle of Bryndal Vale. 

Once placed, a warrior vows to stand their ground upon the Oathstone, or die in the attempt. Many suffer the latter fate, and are rewarded for their sacrifice by having the Oathstone placed upon their grave, its power protecting their remains for eternity. In contrast, a warrior who abandons an Oathstone to the enemy has shamed themselves in the eyes of their ancestors, and will commonly take the Slayer Oath to atone. 

In combat, a Character can sacrifice their Move for the Turn to place and stand upon an Oathstone. So long as you remain standing upon an Oathstone: 

- You also gain a +20 bonus on any Tests to resist forced movement, including Tests to resist gaining the _Broken_ Condition; 

- Enemies do not gain bonus attack modifiers for outnumbering you in melee, or for attacking you in the side or rear; 

- You suffer a -20 penalty on all Dodge Skill Tests. 

## **Anvil of Doom**
It is said the ancestors of the Runesmith Clans used the Anvils of Doom when crafting the most powerful runic items in Dwarf history. Over the millennia, many Anvils of Doom have been lost, or split apart by the raging magic housed within them, but most Karaks still have at least one of these treasures remaining. Few Runesmiths are trusted to work upon an Anvil of Doom, and fewer still are permitted to take them into battle. But those who do so wield one of the greatest weapons at the Dwarfs’ disposal, hammering Doom Runes upon its gromril surface, unleashing their magical power with immediate and explosive force. 

Any Character working magical runes upon an Anvil of Doom gains +20 to all Runesmithing Extended Tests. In addition, any Dwarf within 2 yards of an Anvil of Doom gains +20 on Tests to dispel magic with _Magic Resistance_ ( **WFRP Core Rulebook** ). The Anvil of Doom is the only surface upon which a Dwarf can strike a Doom Rune (page 132). 

Characters positioned behind an Anvil of Doom gain the benefit of hard cover. The Anvil of Doom itself is functionally _Unbreakable_ , though some disasters have tested and overcome this indestructibility, mostly due to excessive use of Doom Runes within a single battle. 

An Anvil of Doom cannot be inscribed with additional runes, as it already bears as much magical power as any runic item can withstand. 

An Oathstone can be inscribed with Talismanic Runes and/or Protection Runes. 

**I** IVI 

## Dwarf Artillery
A Dwarf throng rarely goes into battle without war machines to cover their advance. Like any ranged weapon, artillery can only be used if you have the right Skill Specialisation (with the exceptions noted on **WFRP Core Rulebook** ). Catapults are a new Weapon Group that can only be used if you have the Ranged (Catapult) Skill. Unlike Human Engineering weapons, not every Dwarf Engineering weapon uses blackpowder — the _Blackpowder_ and _Damaging_ 

Qualities only apply to Engineering weapons if explicitly listed in their profile. 

The Dawi were the first to use gunpowder for anything beyond fireworks. Even before Cathay, Karaz Ankor was deploying not just arquebuses and swivel guns, but heavy cannon for defence of their holds. While some see use on the battlefield, others are fixed in place to defend mountain pass and fortress gates. Ever inventive, the Dwarfs of Barak Varr have even found a way to use heavy explosives underwater. All weapons in this section require a crew of three and the Ranged (Engineering) Skill. For each crew member lacking the appropriate skill, or for every skilled crew member below the required number, the Test is made at a (-10) penalty.

**I** IVI 

## **Swivel Gun**
Sometimes called the ‘Halfling’s Cannon’, the swivel gun is somewhere between a large blunderbuss and a small artillery weapon. It consists of two pieces, the gun itself and a heavy, collapsible tripod as a mount. When loaded, it can fire almost any shot, from a single small cannonball to multiple small lead bullets to even rocks. When firing multiple projectiles, the swivel gun has the **Blast (2)** Quality. Effective use of the swivel gun requires two trained crew with the Ranged (Swivel Gun) Skill, one to fire the gun, the other to set up the tripod. Of limited use on the open battlefield, the swivel gun is popular for use in tunnels, defending fortifications from assault, and as anti-personnel weapons on the ships of Barak Varr. 

## **Bombard**
A small cannon that fires lead shot the size of a Dawi’s fist, Dwarfs value the bombard for delivering a punch while still easily portable. A crew of two Dwarfs can carry it to a new location and set it up in 1d3 rounds. It can then be fired on the next round. Both gunners must have the Ranged (Bombard) Skill. A single crewman can operate the bombard, but not move it, and the reload time is doubled. 

## **Mortar**
Squat like a Dwarf, the mortar is a short-barreled cannon meant for indirect fire. Launching a cannonball on a high, arching trajectory, it can hit targets otherwise protected by being behind buildings, forests, or fortifications. While a line of sight to the target is not necessary, all shots from a mortar are a **Hard (-20)** Test, unless there is a spotter to relay precise information about the target. The mortar crew consists of two Dwarfs, each of whom has the Ranged (Mortar) Skill. 

## **Cannon**
The typical artillery piece of Karaz Ankor’s armies, the cannon is similar to those used by the Empire, an unsurprising fact given the assistance of Imperial Dwarfs in the gunnery school at Nuln. They are, however, more reliable, as the Karaz Ankor Engineers Guild is fond of pointing out. A Dwarf field cannon only misfires on an even-numbered double that is also a failed roll. Barak Varr makes use of a somewhat larger version on its heavy ships, called the ‘Tempest’ cannon, with 50% greater range and an additional D+2. 

## Illegal Experiments
Rogue Engineers who defy Dwarf Law and tradition are an occasional problem for all Dwarf holds. One such is ‘Mad’ Alfrik Nunhesson of Karak Norn in the Grey Mountains, who developed a new combination weapon, a poleaxe incorporating a repeating handgun. In spite of occasional problems in testing — the occasional misfire and lost finger or hand is to be expected, after all — Alfrik submitted his design to the Engineer Clan Elders, fully expecting praise and approval. 

He was shocked, insulted, and furious. 

Ordered to cease work and destroy his prototypes as ‘dangerous innovations’, Alfrik left in a huff and set up shop in Ubersreik, where a debt of honour owed by a local Dwarf community have kept him from being harassed. Setting up there as a blacksmith and gunsmith, Alfrik eventually perfected his design. 

That has caused problems for Karak Norn, where the guild entered a formal grudge against Alfrik, approved by King Brokk Ironpick, himself. He would love to have this weapon for his guard, but he is not about to admit he was wrong. And now the manlings have heard of it — rumour has reached the Dwarf king that the Nuln Gunnery School has wind of Alfrik’s invention and has sent agents to lure him to Nuln. 

The Characters are Dwarf of Karak Norn or their manling agents, sent to Ubersreik to convince Alfrik to mend his ways and return home. If he agrees to apologise to the King Brokk, he will have his invention approved and his workshop restored. But Alfrik is more stubborn than most Dwarfs. If he does not agree, the Characters are authorised to steal his plans, destroy his weapons, and kidnap him. Will the Dwarfs of Ubersreik intervene to honour their debt? And what of the agents from Nuln? If they cannot buy Alfrik’s service, what will they resort to? 

**I** IVI 

## **Bolt Thrower**
Dwarf Bolt Throwers are scaled up versions of Dwarf Crossbows, and equally popular with traditionalist Engineers. Though not as sophisticated as Elven Bolt Throwers, they are sturdier and faster-firing than Human Ballistae, thanks to their adaptations to accommodate more crew. Karak Norn makes especially prevalent use of their Bolt Throwers to hunt Great Eagles circling the Grey Mountains, allegedly to aggravate their neighbours in Athel Loren. 

## **Flame Cannon**
Seemingly just another field cannon at first glance, the flame cannon is an unpleasant surprise for enemies when it belches forth a ball of fire into their closely packed lines. Though meant solely for use above ground because of the dangers fire presents in tunnels, refugees from the fall of Karak Drazh told how King Vikram Ironside made a last stand with his warriors in the Great Hall, giving their lives to buy time for others to escape. According to some, the Dwarfking placed all his flame cannons in front of his line and, when the greenskins charged, gave the order to fire. No survivors told what happened next, but the collapse of the mountaintop gave a strong hint. 

## **Volley Gun**
Rather than a cranked circle of tubes, as with Imperial volley Guns, the Dwarf volley gun is a smaller, more ‘intimate’ version of the organ gun. It fires a blast of lead musket balls from up to ten barrels at once. Often mounted on a wheeled carriage for mobility on the battlefield, the volley gun serves to savagely rip through a charging enemy before they can come into contact with the Dwarf lines. The volley gun requires a crew of two with the Ranged (Blackpowder) Skill. A crew of one can fire it with no penalty, but the reload time is doubled, nor can it be moved. 

## **Grudge Thrower**
Dwarf catapults are formidable metal contraptions, as difficult to shift as their famously stubborn crew. Since the War of Vengeance, it has been tradition to inscribe grudges directly onto a catapult’s stone ammunition, with the war machine allegedly rewarding the most righteous grudges with the most accurate shots. Not all crews are so sentimental — hence the ‘Gob-Lobber’ variant, an answer in kind to Goblin ‘Doom Diver’ catapults, that uses live Goblin ammunition.. 

**I** IVI 

## **Organ Gun**
The organ gun consists of five light cannons set on a frame and designed to fire in a volley, though each may fire individually, too. Not as powerful as the field cannon, but moreso than the volley gun, the combined fire of an organ gun can shred the packed lines of an enemy force. 

## **Goblin-Hewer**
The latest invention of the Slayer-Engineer Malakai Makaisson is an automatic, axe-propelling, war machine that delivers whole armouries of scything blades into enemy formations at lethal speed. Like all of Malakai’s inventions, the Goblin-hewer has been denounced by the Engineers Guild, who consider it an insult to the artillery designs perfected by the ancestors generations ago. Yet the machine’s effectiveness at obliterating tight-packs of enemy soldiers has inspired countless imitators, despite the Guild’s admonishment. 

## **Weapon Installations**
Some weapons are too heavy to be carried or wheeled into battle, even by Dwarfs. Other weapons are only suitable when fired from the range and vantage point of skycraft. The weapons below can be found installed in Dwarfen vehicles or fortifications, and cannot usually be operated except when occupying those positions. Though they usually cannot be purchased separately from the vehicles that mount them, the table includes Prices and Availabilities to provide a guideline when exchanging one weapon installation with another.

**I** IVI 

## **Clattergun**
Clatterguns are rapid-firing repeater handguns, similar in some ways to a Swivel Gun. They are lighter than a Gyrocopter’s conventional armament, improving the vehicle’s capacity for explosive munitions. 

## **Breaker Cannon**
The breaker is the standard gun on Barak Varr’s ships and is a lighter version of the field cannon. There have been experiments with dismounting these guns and taking them ashore with Dwarf landing parties that move out of range of a ship’s guns, but this is still considered an insufficiently tested innovation. 

## **Tempest Cannon**
Barak Varr makes use of a somewhat larger version on its heavy ships, called the ‘Tempest’ cannon, with 50% greater range and an additional D+2. 

## **Thunder Cannon**
The thunder cannon is the largest gun Karaz Ankor produces, so heavy that it cannot travel with an army. Instead, this cannon guards the gates and mountain passes leading to the Dwarf Empire’s holds. Mounted in fortified casements on the sides of mountains, its crew of five operates carefully engineered clockworks and steampowered hydraulics to control its aim and elevation. In addition to the Ranged (Engineering) Skill to fire, properly operating the aiming mechanisms requires a successful **Challenging (+0) Trade (Engineering)** Test. On a failure, each -1 SL counts as a -10 penalty to the **Ranged (Engineering)** Test. 

## **Steam Gun**
Originally designed to relieve pressure on a Gyrocopter’s steam engine, the Engineers Guild quickly realised the military applications for an expanding cloud of scalding water vapour. Before discharging a Steam Gun, Gyrocopter pilots must carefully position their vehicle to compensate for the weapon’s short range, whilst still avoiding retaliation from the blistered survivors. 

## **Brimstone Gun**
## **Aerial Bombs**
Both Gyrocopters and war Balloons can carry aerial bombs. Though less powerful than a standard bomb, several raining from above can still terrorise an enemy. As a dropped weapon, the bomb’s range is irrelevant. Aerial bombs are smaller, however, and so do less damage. 

## **Grudgebuster Bomb**
A heavier payload designed for dedicated bombing craft, Grudgebuster Bombs are designed to ‘bounce’ on impact with the ground, setting off a cluster of secondary explosions. A successful chain reaction of blasts will devastate a tightly packed formation, but the results are somewhat unpredictable. 

## Steamcraft
The invention of the steam engine has proven crucial to Karaz Ankor’s survival. From mining tools to flying machines (see **Skycraft** ) to ships of war (see **Watercraft** ), steam engines amplify the power of the Dwarfs and make up for their declining numbers. 

For something so invaluable to the Dwarfs, it surprises many to learn that the steam engine has its origins in children’s toys. 

According to the records of the Engineers Guild, the first steam engine appeared in the workshops of Dargo Grindolsson in the 8th century IC. A member of the Roedtfjell clan of Karaz-a-Karak, Grindolsson focused on the making of toys both for the young of the Karaks and the children of the nobility in the growing Empire to the west. When listening to a kettle whistle one day, he wondered if he could harness that power to make things move. Experimenting first with a simple steam boiler that spun when steam was forced through nozzles, Grindolsson soon devised more complex steam-powered toys to amuse young and old, such as a colourful carousel of griffons ridden by knights — a big hit in the Empire — and a Dwarf headsman who would behead a Goblin king over and over. 

Since the development of drakefire, some Gyrocopter pilots have exchanged their Steam Gun for this new armament — preferring to take the risk on newer technology for the advantage of improved range and stopping power. 

**I** IVI 

It was the news of the fall of Karaz Azgal to the dragon Graug that set Dargo to wondering how his steam engines could aid the Dwarfs, not just amuse them. Soon he was proposing all sorts of inventions to the Guild Elders to make mining more productive — steam drills and hammers, steam pumps and presses, even a mechanical steam-powered miner. Already sceptical, the Elders nearly spit their beer when he proposed a steamdriven tunnel-borer that could also function as a troop carrier, and even presented drawings for an outlandish steam-powered flying machine. 

But Dargo had an ally — the High King. The failure of the expedition to recover Karak Azgal and the many Dwarfs lost in the effort weighed heavily on him. Though his High Council mocked Grindolsson’s ideas and recommended he be dismissed as a loony, the High King overruled them and ordered Dargo to proceed. 

Operators may be required to Test when moving at accelerated speeds, negotiating difficult terrain, attempting an unusual manoeuvre, or engaging in a dangerous pursuit. 

Vehicles suffer Damage in the same way as Characters. Their Toughness Bonus reduces the amount of Damage taken, and their Wounds indicate much Damage they can withstand before destruction. Attacks against vehicles usually gain a bonus due to the vehicle’s Enormous or Monstrous Size, and in melee are opposed by the driver’s Drive, Row, or Sail Skill (as appropriate). If a melee attack is made against a stationary vehicle, or a vehicle the attacker is on board, the defender does not roll and counts as scoring –10 SL. The effects of Criticals, or called shots, should be improvised according to the vehicle’s specific components — you’ll find suggestions throughout this chapter. 

It was a wise choice. Though not without early failures, Dargo’s designs showed enough promise that other workshops began developing their own steam devices, leading to their widespread use in Karaz Ankor and across other holds. 

## **Vehicle Rules**
The steamcraft, skycraft, and watercraft in this chapter all use the same vehicle profile. Vehicle Crew indicates the number of trained individuals required to operate the vehicle effectively. Encumbrance measures the weight and bulk of the vehicle itself. Carry Capacity states how many Encumbrance points of cargo the vehicle can easily hold (all vehicle handling Tests suffer a –1 penalty for each 10% by which this capacity is exceeded). Movement details how many yards-per-Turn it moves in combat, and miles-per-hour for long distance travel. Testing Drive, Row, or Sail is usually unnecessary when travelling. 

Lasting repairs to a vehicle require specialist facilities and a team of professionals, but a Character with appropriate Trade Tools can implement temporary repairs. This is a **Difficult (−10) Trade (Engineering)** Test (or other relevant Trade Specialisation) to restore 1d10+SL Wounds to the vehicle, or undo the effects of a Critical. These problems return at the end of the adventure. 

Several **WFRP** supplements provide more detailed vehicle rules, including additional Critical effects, customisation options, the impact of weather or other hazards, and Endeavours suitable for long-distance vehicle travel. If you would like to furnish your vehicles with this additional level of detail, recommended supplements include the **Enemy in Shadow Companion** (for land vehicles), **Enemy in Ruins** (for air vehicles), and **Sea of Claws** (for water vehicles).

**I** IVI 

## **Intellectual Theft**
Though happy to help the Dawi and proud of the honours the High King showered upon him, Dargo was shocked and angered when the High King ordered that the secret of the steam engine and his other plans be shared not only within Karaz-a-Karak, but even with the other holds of Karaz Ankor. Though he loudly protested this theft of his property, all the High King would say was that his innovation would be of great use to Dwarfs throughout Karaz Ankor. Finally, after repeated protestations, Dargo so irritated the High King that he was barred from the Royal Presence, denied even the respect due any Dawi. As time passed, the Dwarfs of the other holds stopped consulting him or even acknowledging his pioneering work. 

Filled with shame at his humiliation, Dargo was left with one recourse. Shaving his head and turning his keys over to his Chief Apprentice, Dargo Grindolsson took the oath of the Slayer, picked up his axe, and left for Troll Country, never to be seen again. 

## **Earth Borer Mining Drill**
Grindolsson’s original design called for a gigantic steel drill bit mounted on a heavy cannon carriage whose wheels could be locked in place. A steam engine also mounted on the carriage would turn the drill, though the borer itself had to be wheeled into position by hand. A tragic accident that led to the deaths of several Dwarfs showed the dangers of the drill overheating, thus a crew was added to run a pump and spray water on the drill to cool it. 

Dwarf engineers eventually worked out a complex mechanism to use the steam engine to also drive the wheels and power a built-in water cooling pump, making the Earth Borer self-propelled. This reduced the crew needed for each borer from a dozen Dwarfs to just four. Crews now compete with each other to see who can dig the deepest new tunnels the fastest. 

While digging tunnels to find new resources, it was inevitable that Earth Borer crews would encounter Skaven. The first response was to armour the carriage to protect the crew, but soon the Dawi thought of offensive uses. Building larger, extended versions of the Earth Borer, Dwarf Engineers turned them into troop carriers and assault vehicles. Able to carry up to a dozen armoured 

Dwarfs in addition to the crew, the ‘War Borers’ are used to raid Skaven lairs, surprising them by attacking from new directions through freshly dug tunnels. The latest models can even drop explosives to collapse tunnels as the borer withdraws at the end of a raid. 

Earth Borers with a Drill Bit can carve a path directly through solid rock, though they reduce their Move to 1 whilst doing so. A Critical hit against an Earth Borer jams its drilling mechanism, immobilising its progress through the earth, and overloading its steam boiler if the jam is not cleared. 

## **Kolbrokdul Mining Carriage**
Originally designed by the Kolbrukdul clan workshop of Zhufbar, the steam-powered mining carriage enables Dwarf miners to bring up more ore more quickly to the processing shops and forges. At first ore was transported by Dwarfs in great bags on their backs, and later by carts pushed by hand along tracks. While this is still done at smaller, more distant mines and holds, or in side tunnels not wide enough for a carriage, the clank of a carriage’s engines and the sight of it moving along a main shaft is common at the great holds. Even Karak Norn and Karak Izor have started using them, gifts from the High King to paper-over a grudge. In recent years the Dwarfs have also pressed them into service as ambulances, carrying wounded Dwarfs rescued from a battle or from a cave-in to receive treatment in safer areas. 

The Mining Carriage has a driver, who works the gears and tiller to steer it and control the engine. It can carry up to 500 pounds of ore, or a half-dozen wounded Dawi. 

## Runaway Drill
Dawi Characters testing a new drill design are taken for a ride when the controls stick and the engine runs amok. The out-of-control borer drills deeper and deeper into the earth, below the deepest mines and far beyond where any known Dawi has explored. Eventually, the borer’s engine burns itself out and comes to a halt in a vast, strange cavern unlike any the Dwarfs have seen before. What have they found? A gromril motherlode? A Skaven city? The final resting place of Grungni and Valaya? 

And how do they get back? 

**I** IVI 

Mining Carriages move along pre-laid rail tracks. A Critical hit against a Mining Carriage derails it, immobilising the vehicle until it is lifted back onto the track. Additional mine carts can be connected to a mining carriage — each cart improves Carry Capacity by 100, but reduces Move by 1. 

If a party is lucky enough to travel along a Stage of a delve via Mining Carriage (which is only possible in a few well-travelled sections of the Underway), they may choose to make a **Challenging (+0) Drive** Test to ignore the effect of a Delving Encounter, by outpacing or circumnavigating the hazard. 

## Skycraft

- _’Go up in one of those? You’re as mad as an Elf! A Dwarf ’s feet belong firmly on stone or safely under it, not a mile up with nothing between them and the ground!’_ 

Earthquakes shattered the Great Underway in several places, choking the tunnels with millions of tons of rubble, while other portions were seized by the Skaven. Greenkins and Trolls overran the surface ways rendering them unsafe for all but large armies. Holds could be cut off for years at a time, until they fell, or relief came. Even though the Dawi would push back and reopen routes, there was always the risk of the enemy cutting them again. They needed another way. 

Dwarfs had used balloons for many years, rising above the mountain passes to keep an eye on the lands below for signs of enemies. Tethered to a high peak, an observer in a balloon would send messages in a cylinder that slid along a rope. There were some attempts to use these balloons to travel between holds, but it was slow and the winds unpredictable. When a change in the winds stranded the Dwarfking of Karak Kadrin at the edge of the Dark Lands, the idea of using balloons for transportation was quickly dropped. 

—Gomrund Forkbeard, Dwarf diplomat and traditionalist 

The war that ended the Golden Age failed to bring down Karaz Ankor — but only just. But, while the Empire held, the volcanic eruptions, earthquakes, and rampaging armies of Skaven and greenskins disrupted communications the length of the Dwarf empire. 

The invention of the steam engine changed that. Adding both increased speed and a measure of control regardless of the winds, steam-powered lighter-than-air craft came to be gradually accepted. Three types are most common in Karaz Ankor — the airship or dirigible, the gyrocopter, and the war balloon. 

**I** IVI 

## **Airship**
## **What’s Mine Is Mine**
Dawi have strong ideas about property rights, especially when it comes to the products of their own craftsmanship and labour. When a Dwarf spends years making a complex piece of technology, from a submersible to a gyrocopter to a musket, making it not only functional, but beautiful, it becomes something very personal to them. Each Dwarf Engineer, therefore, feels a very real sense of ownership over his creation and is reluctant to hand it over to another, unless it was a commissioned work, or ordered to do so at the command of a Dwarfking. Dwarfs have a hard time describing it, but tell Humans to imagine giving away a part of their own body. This conflict was at the heart of Dargo Grindolsson’s anguish. 

But this possessiveness does not apply to everything. Common, everyday items do not evoke this response. Thus Humans who have heard wild tales of the Dwarfs’ legendary greed are surprised when a Dwarf has no problem letting them borrow a hammer. They are equally surprised when the Dwarf reacts in outrage at an offer to buy their handcrafted blunderbuss. 

Dwarf Skycraft are piloted with the Sail (Skycraft) Skill (page 80). Unlike other vehicles, the experimental nature of skycraft dictates that the pilot must always take an **Average (+20) Sail (Skycraft)** Test during take-off and landing, with failed Tests delaying arrival/departure, or inflicting damage on the vehicle/its occupants/the landing zone. A Critical hit against a flying vehicle results in a sudden loss of altitude — startling and nauseating the crew at best, triggering a crash with nearby terrain at worst. 

An evolutionary development of the War Balloon, the airship or ‘dirigible’ is a lighter-than-air vehicle used as transport by dignitaries when land travel is inconvenient or dangerous. Dawi envoys consider them especially handy when trying to impress local Humans. _‘Nothing makes an impression like dropping in from above’_ , said one Dwarf ambassador when arriving for negotiations in Talabheim. And, unlike gromril treasures, Dwarf Kings are not averse to commissioning one occasionally as a gift for a Human lord when he needs to impress and flatter one. Baron Heinrich’s dirigible, ( _**Empire in** ‘The Sky Wolf ’_ _**Ruins**_ , page 37), is a famous example, commissioned by the Dwarfs of Middenheim . 

The airship consists of a gondola the size of a barge suspended from a large, sausage shaped balloon filled with air heated by the steam engine. The gondolas are either open to the air or enclosed, but they are always elegantly made and furnished. Open-air gondolas have a cabin passengers can retreat to in inclement weather. Propulsion can be wind-driven, though this is slow. Most make use of the steam engine, which drives a twinbladed screw that pushes the dirigible along, even against moderately strong winds. Steering is accomplished by means of twin rudders in front of the bow, which are in turn controlled by a series of cables attached to a pilot’s wheel. While an airship can climb as high as 2,000 feet, most cruise much lower, unless danger on the ground mandates climbing. The typical dirigible has a crew of six — two pilots, two engineers, and two general hands for maintenance, ropes, and cargo handling.

While not designed as a warship, a dirigible has ports for small cannon such as the swivel gun. Larger weapons tend to make the gondola into an unstable platform. 

Airships are miraculous creations, each one-of-a-kind, with their size, shape, and armament determined by the whims of the Engineer creators. The Skycraft table provides baseline profiles for Dwarf dirigibles of three different sizes. Small airships, such as those docked aboard a _Grudgebreaker_ -class battleship, are often surprisingly well-armed for their size, packing a pair of prow-mounted Breaker Cannons. Medium airships, such as the _Sky Wolf_ gifted to the city of Middenheim (see **Empire in Ruins** ) are more commonly used for transportation, though racks of Aerial Bombs are not uncommon. The largest Airships, such as the _Spirit of Grungni_ created by slayer-engineer Malakai Makaisson, can transport whole formations of Dwarf warriors, and are equipped with Organ Gun broadsides. 

## **Gyrocopter and Variants**
_’It’s just like riding a horse, except you don’t usually get back on after falling off.’_ 

—A Dawi gyrocopter pilot to an Imperial cavalryman 

One of the Dwarfs’ most ingenious inventions, the gyrocopter evokes wonder from all who see it, as well as exclamations of shock and awe. 

Gyrocopters are an invention of the Dwarf Engineers’ Guild. As the legend goes, the inventor was inspired by the sight of a Dragon swooping over the Worlds Edge Mountains. He thought that the engines used to drive steam-powered drilling machinery might provide the necessary thrust, and that adapting flywheels from grinding machines would help power and stabilise the device. His invention proved successful, and whilst it has been much adapted and refined over the centuries since, the basic principles are still employed in the more recent designs. Now only the smaller Dwarf holds or more conservative clans fail to keep a small fleet of Gyrocopters., Because of the time and skill required to make one, as well as the Dawi’s adherence to a workshop model of production, the Dwarfs produce relatively few gyrocopters, and those few are risked sparingly. While now in use in Karaz Ankor and some of the Western holds, the gyrocopter has never been willingly given or sold to an outsider. 

The typical gyrocopter is an open frame of metal and wood with a seat for one pilot, who also operates the steam cannon. Fueled by a highly-efficient coal, a small steam engine powers the propellers used for lift and steering, and also generates steam for the cannon. Before takeoff, the engine is primed with enough coal to last eight hours, or four if repeated use is made of the steam cannon. 

Gyrocopters take-off vertically, and are capable of hovering in place. Most are equipped with a Steam Gun, but some variants replace this weapon with a Brimstone Gun, or strip out the weapon entirely (which increases its Move to 25). The craft’s stabilisers are also fitted with a small payload of Aerial Bombs. 

Gyrobombers are heavier, double-rotored versions of the Gyrocopter, their increased size improving their capacity for munitions. Most are equipped with bouncing, multiexplosive Grudgebuster Bomb racks, and a lighter Clattergun in place of the Gyrocopter’s main weapon. Occasionally, a Gryobomber may be stripped of its bomb racks, and used to deliver emergency relief supplies to besieged holds — this increases its Carry Capacity to 60. 

**I** IVI 

Though it is fuel-intensive, all Gyrocopters can achieve incredible bursts of speed in combat, moving up to 5 times their Move with a **Challenging (+0) Sail (Skycraft)** Test. Failed Tests may place unexpected pressure upon the vehicle’s steam engine, resulting in reduced acceleration or loss of altitude. See the _Flight_ Creature Trait ( **WFRP Core Rulebook** ) for more guidelines about flying combatants, though Gyrocopters cannot take-off and land in combat without expending a Move to do so. 

The success of the gyrocopter has spawned variations geared to a specific purpose. The ‘fast’ gyrocopter is a model built for speed. With no cannon or bombs and made of lighter material, it is 25% faster than the standard gyrocopter, but with a **Toughness** of only 5. Its primary use is for reconnaissance and carrying urgent messages between holds. 

A heavier, slower model is lovingly called ‘Pack Mule’ by its pilots and those to whom it brings needed supplies. Larger than standard, usually unarmed, and with a more powerful steam engine, the undercarriage is fitted with a hook that lets the craft lift a pallet or crate slung by ropes. It can carry up to 300 Enc of packed goods, 250 if armed, but flies 25% slower than the standard gyrocopter. 

## **War Balloon**
The earliest Dwarf aerial vehicle was the balloon. First used at Karak Kadrin in the War of Vengeance to keep an eye out for Elves, they proved their worth in the aftermath of the Skaven and greenskin invasions. Observers posted in tethered outposts high above the approaches to the mountains kept watch and sent warnings to the holds below via message cylinder or semaphore. Eventually an Engineer clan tried adding a small steam engine and propeller, this giving rise to the ‘War Balloon’. 

The War Balloon is simply a gondola of wicker and light metal suspended beneath a balloon by guy ropes that also form a net to hold the balloon’s shape. When powered with an engine and propeller, it is capable of slow flight, even against all but the strongest winds, and carries coal for a week’s travel. This enables the War Balloon to go on scouting missions far beyond the edges of the World’s Edge Mountains through a judicious use of the winds and the steam engine. War Balloons are primarily used for surveillance and reconnaissance, and are painted in neutral colours that blend into the sky, imposing a –20 modifier on enemy Perception Tests to spot them. Their maximum altitude is much higher than a Gyrocopter, and they can be tethered in mid-air when the weather is agreeable. Despite their name, War Balloons are rarely heavily armed, but may carry a complement of Aerial Bombs, along with Handguns and Crossbows for the crew. 

## **Aerial Bombs**
Both Gyrocopters and war Balloons can carry aerial bombs. Though less powerful than a standard bomb, several raining from above can still terrorise an enemy. As a dropped weapon, the bomb’s range is irrelevant. Aerial bombs are smaller, however, and so do less damage. 

## **Conspiracy in the Darklands**
On a balloon scouting mission,the Characters see signs of a camp in remote country where no one was known to live. Aerial observation reveals little, so the Characters must land to scout the situation up close. To their shock, they discover that a party of Chaos Dwarfs is negotiating with a group of Imperial officials — from Sylvania. What are they doing here, so far from home? What happens next is largely up to the Characters. Attacking the camp will not tell them why Sylvanians are talking to the blood enemies of Karaz Ankor. Whether they discover the reason or decide to fly back to Karaz Ankor, their enemies spot them. Can their War Balloon make it back to warn the Dwarfs, or will their enemies find a way to shoot them down? 

**I** IVI 

## Watercraft
_’A key to keeping our remaining tanks in good working order may be in understanding the watercraft of the Dwarfs. They are clad in similar grade and thickness of steel, mount far more artillery, and are similarly propelled through the power of a steam engine. I am sure Miragliano must have had the Ironclad and Monitor in mind when he drafted blueprints for his own land ship. If only the Engineers’ Guilds of our erstwhile allies could be persuaded to share their ideas it might provide our salvation.’_ 

— Engineer Commander Feinkopf, in a lucid moment 

Dwarf ships, let alone a whole armed fleet, are just inconceivable to most people outside Karaz Ankor. The idea that a folk so rooted in the earth, so dedicated to digging ever deeper, could even want to sail the seas, let alone build ships for it, seems laughable on its face. 

And yet building a navy is exactly what one Dwarf hold has done. 

The Hold of Barak Varr is an outlier from the rest of Karaz Ankor in more ways than one. One of the southernmost holds remaining after the fall of Karak Drazh and Karak Azgal, it is also not in the World’s Edge Mountains. 

Instead it sits in the Varenka Hills, where the Skull river flows into the Black Gulf, against the lands of the Border Princes. Some Dawi in the other holds claim this gives the Dwarfs of Barak Varr a strange outlook, more manling than Dwarf. 

Regardless, the reality of the lands and waters around Barak Varr, as well as the dangers they faced, led them to become very good shipbuilders. 

Isolated in the Varenka Hills, Barak Varr’s only connection to the rest of Karaz Ankor is along the Skull River. This waterway flows from a source near the road from KarazA-Karak to Black Fire Pass and enters the Black Gulf near Barak Varr. Though necessary, travel along the river is unsafe, thanks to the dangers posed by raiding greenskins and Humans from the Border Princes. 

The Black Gulf is itself dangerous. Raiders of all sorts have tried to assault Barak Varr from the sea, ranging from Sartosan pirates to the fleet of Skaven that terrorised the coasts along the Gulf and the Great Ocean in 2231 IC. Facing threats no army could touch, Barak Varr decided to build an ‘army of the sea’. 

**I** IVI 

Throwing themselves into the task, the Engineers and workshops of the hold studied captured ships and learned all they could from them. And then they improved them, building a range of ships from those meant for rivers to great steel craft that could travel on and under the Black Gulf. They adapted their weapons for use on the water and invented ones for battles beneath the waves. 

Barak Varr’s ships are equipped to fight at range and up close. The guns of all ships except the gunboat are mounted in sealed turrets to protect the gun crews, while hydraulic mechanisms powered by the ship’s steam plant allows the turret to rotate as needed. This lets the ship swiftly bring its guns to bear on an enemy, rather than turn the entire hull. 

Unique among the peoples of the Old World, the oceangoing ships of the Dwarfs, the Monitors, Ironclads, Dreadnoughts, and submersibles, are all metal, defying and baffling the shipbuilders of other kingdoms. Like other powerful weapons of the Dwarfs, each ship is an individual work of craftsmanship by a Master Naval Engineer of Barak Varr and his apprentices, and experienced sailors can identify not only the type of ship, but the workshop it came from based on its design. 

All Dwarf ships are steam powered, sails having been abandoned once centuries of testing (and letting others take the risks) had shown that they were reliable and could be scaled to the needs of a large craft. Rejecting the propellers that worked so well on airships, the Dwarfs of Barak Varr instead chose to power all their ships save the Nautilus by paddlewheel — a small sternwheel on the river gunboats and great side wheels on the oceangoing ships. Dwarf ships are thus not dependent on the wind. 

Unlike the ships of Humans and Elves, which have open decks and are exposed to the elements, Barak Varr’s metal ships are also completely sealed, from keel to crow’s nest. Access to the crew areas and the storage holds are only through tightly sealed hatches that can be barred from the inside. Not only watertight, this design also keeps out boarders — since the first Ironclads were launched in the 18th century IC, no enemy has ever successfully boarded and captured a Dwarf ocean ship. 

Like their land-bound cousins, the Dwarfs of Barak Varr like to get up close and personal in a fight. All Dwarf ships other than the gunboat are equipped with steel rams meant to punch holes in the enemy’s wooden hulls, the Dwarf ship pulling back and striking again and again until the enemy sinks. Few captains have the courage — or are sufficiently insane — to face an oncoming Ironclad as its steamwhistle bellows a challenge. 

Rams play a role in boarding actions, too. When a captain decides it is better to capture a ship as a prize than sink it, he rams it once to hold it in place. Then the crew swing a hydraulic ramp into place, across which a squad of axe and hammer-wielding Dwarfs charge to seize the other vessel. Many see it as proof that Dwarfs who go to sea are ‘not quite right in the head’, because they charge in full armour — over the open ocean! 

Dwarf Watercraft are piloted with the Sail Skill. Each Watercraft has its own Specialisation, but a Character with Advances in any Sail Specialisation treats all other Sail Specialisations as Basic Skills. Critical hits against boats might inflict penalties to Sail Tests, deal 9 Damage to occupants due to flying splinters, or even cause the boat to take on water.
